title: Periodic Unitary Encoding for Quantum Anomaly Detection of Temporal Series
journal_or_venue: Proceedings of the 1st International Conference on Quantum Software (IQSOFT 2025)
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a quantum kernel for unsupervised anomaly detection in time series that embeds known seasonality by encoding data with a periodic unitary induced by a Hamiltonian whose period matches the task seasonality. Instantaneous, time-dependent quantum feature maps are combined into a composite kernel for One-Class SVMs; experiments on the NYC Taxi Request dataset show that using a Hamiltonian with the correct period (7) improves detection performance over random or period-1 choices and yields results competitive with DTW, while a classical RBF kernel achieved the best overall performance in this task.
methodology_description: The authors propose a quantum-kernel based method for unsupervised anomaly detection in time series that explicitly incorporates known seasonality. They build instantaneous quantum kernels for each time step by encoding the classical features xt with a fixed feature map U(xt) and then applying a time-dependent unitary U(t)=exp(-i H t) induced by a Hamiltonian H whose eigenvalues are chosen as (coprime) integers so that U(t) is periodic with the desired seasonality. Instantaneous kernels kt(xt,yt) are combined as a weighted sum K = sum_t alpha_t kt (weights chosen heuristically or via classical Multiple Kernel Learning such as EasyMKL). The quantum kernel value is the squared overlap κ(x,y)=|<φ(x)|φ(y)>|^2 where φ(xt,t)=U(xt) exp(-i H t)|0>^n. Kernels are computed by simulating 2-qubit noiseless circuits (angle encoding RX(xπ) for U(xt)) with periodic Hamiltonians (integer eigenvalues sampled uniformly from {-15,...,15}). The combined kernel is used with a classical One-Class SVM trained only on non-anomalous windows; hyperparameters (ν and decision threshold) are selected by maximizing balanced accuracy on a validation split. Experiments compare quantum kernels with varying periodicities (random, period-1, period-7) against classical baselines (linear, polynomial, RBF kernels) and a DTW-based method. Each experiment is repeated 30 times and performance is reported by mean ± std for Precision, Recall, F1 and Balanced Accuracy.
algorithms_used: Classical SVMs with linear, polynomial, RBF kernels
experimental_setup: 2-qubit quantum circuits simulated in a noiseless environment using Qiskit. Data encoded with angle rotations RX(x * π). Periodic Hamiltonians constructed from integer eigenvalues sampled uniformly from {-15,...,15}. Each experiment repeated 30 times. One-Class SVM trained classically; hyperparameters chosen by validation maximizing balanced accuracy.

experiment_input.source: Kaggle (Jul 2014 - Jan 2015 aggregated counts every 30 minutes)
experiment_input.preprocessing: Time series are split into windows corresponding to 7 days. A window is labeled anomalous if it contains one of five documented anomalous days (NYC Marathon Nov 2, Thanksgiving Nov 27, Christmas Dec 25, New Year's Day Jan 1, Blizzard Jan 27). Non-anomalous weeks used for training; remaining samples (including anomalies) used for validation/test.
experiment_input.notes: The dataset is not financial data (included here because original experiment used this public transport dataset).

pipeline_steps: Split the time series into 7-day windows; label windows anomalous if containing any documented anomalous day.
Partition data: from non-anomalous windows, 70% used for training. Remaining samples (including anomalies) are split 30%/70% into validation and test sets respectively.
For each time step t in a window, encode feature xt using angle encoding RX(x * π) on 2 qubits to produce U(xt)|0>^n.
Apply time-dependent unitary exp(-i H t) where H is constructed to yield a desired period (random H, 1-period, or 7-period).

Form instantaneous quantum feature states φ(xt,t) and build instantaneous kernels kt; combine into final kernel K = sum_t alpha_t kt (weights either uniform with periodic constraints or could be optimized via classical MKL).
Compute quantum kernel entries by simulating overlaps (noiseless Qiskit simulation).
Train a classical One-Class SVM on the training kernel matrix (only non-anomalous samples).
Select SVM hyperparameters (ν and threshold) by maximizing balanced accuracy on validation set.
Evaluate on test set and compute Precision, Recall, F1, Balanced Accuracy; repeat entire experiment 30 times to obtain mean±std.

key_findings: [supported] A quantum kernel that embeds seasonality via a periodic unitary (constructed from a Hamiltonian with coprime integer eigenvalues) can be implemented and used in a One-Class SVM pipeline for anomaly detection in time series.

[supported] On the Taxi Request dataset, a quantum temporal kernel using a 7-period Hamiltonian (7-P) outperformed other tested quantum kernels (random Hamiltonian and 1-P Hamiltonian) in balanced accuracy and F1 score.
[supported] Classical RBF and DTW baselines achieved equal or better performance than the tested quantum kernels on this anomaly-detection task (RBF produced the best overall balanced accuracy).
[supported] The proposed quantum-kernel approach was implemented within the CSIMQE-style workflow (quantum resources used only to compute kernels, classical training thereafter).
[supported] The experiments were run with 2-qubit noiseless Qiskit simulations and repeated (30 runs) to produce the reported metrics.

[speculative] Choosing Hamiltonian eigenvalues as coprime integers guarantees a desired periodicity of the induced unitary and thus enforces seasonality-consistent encodings (paper provides a theoretical construction and discussion).

[speculative] Optimizing the Hamiltonian parameters may be unnecessary because random parameter choices often perform comparably in related QML settings (authors cite prior work to motivate not optimizing in this unsupervised setting).
[speculative] Embedding known periodicity/seasonality into quantum kernels is likely to be more beneficial for tasks with stronger time-dependent structure than the tested Taxi Request task.

[speculative] The periodic unitary encoding technique has potential applications beyond anomaly detection (e.g., building equivariances under translations) and could be applied whenever domain knowledge about periodicity is available.

[speculative] Selecting kernel combination weights α_i such that α_i = α_{i+P} yields invariance under P-step translations (theoretical property used to incorporate seasonality into the final kernel).
results_summary: The paper proposes a periodic-unitary-based quantum kernel that encodes seasonality into instantaneous encodings and composes them into a kernel for One-Class SVM anomaly detection. Empirical evaluation on the NYC Taxi Request dataset (2-qubit noiseless simulations, 30 trials) shows the kernel using a Hamiltonian with a 7-step period improves over other quantum variants (random and 1-P) but does not surpass the best classical baseline (RBF). The method is implemented as a CSIMQE-style hybrid (quantum kernel computation followed by classical SVM training) and the authors argue the approach is promising especially when prior knowledge of seasonality is available.
performance_claims: 7-P Hamiltonian (quantum): Precision = 0.860 ± 0.272, Recall = 0.678 ± 0.297, F1 = 0.733 ± 0.263, Balanced Accuracy = 0.816 ± 0.148.
Random Hamiltonian (quantum): Precision = 0.764 ± 0.376, Recall = 0.589 ± 0.358, F1 = 0.630 ± 0.329, Balanced Accuracy = 0.761 ± 0.170.
1-P Hamiltonian (quantum): Precision = 0.721 ± 0.396, Recall = 0.578 ± 0.381, F1 = 0.610 ± 0.356, Balanced Accuracy = 0.756 ± 0.185.
Dynamic Time Warping (classical): Precision = 0.882 ± 0.156, Recall = 0.800 ± 0.241, F1 = 0.802 ± 0.155, Balanced Accuracy = 0.850 ± 0.111.
RBF kernel (classical): Precision = 0.941 ± 0.122, Recall = 0.778 ± 0.295, F1 = 0.814 ± 0.222, Balanced Accuracy = 0.869 ± 0.153.
Experimental setup: kernels computed with 2-qubit circuits, simulated noiselessly using Qiskit; each experiment was repeated 30 times.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not claim a demonstrated quantum advantage over classical methods; the best quantum variant (7-P) improved over other quantum variants but was outperformed by classical RBF on the tested anomaly-detection task. The authors present the method as a domain-informed quantum encoding rather than a claim of computational advantage.
limitations: Computation of gradients for learning the Hamiltonian can be infeasible due to trainability issues and the need for efficient gradient computation (author-stated).
Learning/optimizing the Hamiltonian typically requires a supervised setting, which may not be available for anomaly detection tasks (author-stated).
Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL) techniques used to optimize kernel coefficients typically rely on supervised data and thus may not be suitable for unsupervised anomaly detection (author-stated).
Barren plateau phenomena and related issues limit the feasibility of variational / gradient-based quantum approaches (author-stated).
Random parameter selection may perform comparably to optimized parameters in similar kernels, reducing the benefit of expensive optimization (author-stated).

On the Taxi Requests anomaly detection task studied, a classical RBF kernel outperformed the proposed quantum approach, indicating the quantum model may not always give practical gains on every dataset (author-stated).
The Dynamic Time Warping baseline is not a positive-definite kernel, limiting its formal interpretation as a kernel method (author-stated).

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — Combine quantum temporal kernels (instantaneous feature maps with time-dependent periodic unitaries) with classical One-Class SVM and MKL weighting to perform unsupervised anomaly detection on time-series windows.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Encoding known seasonality via a periodic Hamiltonian (7-period) improves detection performance relative to mis-specified/random periodicities and yields performance competitive with DTW baselines on the tested dataset, though the best classical RBF kernel still outperforms the quantum kernel.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Demonstrated end-to-end pipeline using 2-qubit angle-encoding circuits simulated in Qiskit (noiseless), with code released, indicating a small-scale proof-of-concept implementable on current simulators and possibly small NISQ devices with further validation.
#limitation:qubit-count — Experiments are limited to 2 qubits, raising questions about scalability to real-world, higher-dimensional financial time-series.
#limitation:simulation-only — All kernel overlaps and experiments are performed with noiseless classical simulation (Qiskit); no real QPU experiments were run.
#limitation:noise — The impact of hardware noise and error mitigation is not assessed, so practicality on NISQ hardware is uncertain.
contradictions: Paper reports that a seasonality-aware quantum kernel (7-period) improves over other quantum kernel choices and is competitive with DTW, but a classical RBF kernel achieves the best overall performance — undermining any strong claim of quantum superiority on the tested task.
